concepts.def: The changing family: rising divorce, blended and single-parent families, and new family models in German-speaking society.
The digital world: how the internet, smartphones and social media are reshaping daily life and relationships.
Migration into German-speaking countries and its effects on society, the economy and culture.
Integration: how newcomers become part of society, debated alongside multiculturalism and identity.
Equality, especially between men and women, in work, family and public life as a current social trend.
Demographic change: an ageing population and falling birth rate, with major social consequences.

walkthroughs.body_html:
Aspects of German-speaking Society: Current Trends — a core area of A-Level German.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Aspects of German-speaking Society: Current Trends brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Aspects of German-speaking Society: Current Trends.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: What does 'die Familie im Wandel' describe?
options: The changing nature of the family in society
A family holiday
A type of house
A German verb
Equality (e.g. between men and women)
A train timetable
A school subject
A type of food

mcqs.q: Which is an example of 'der demografische Wandel'?
options: An ageing population and low birth rate
A new mobile phone
A football match
A music festival

mcqs.q: 'Die Migration' as a social trend means:
options: The movement of people into the country
A bird species
A grammar rule
A holiday abroad
A school subject
Equality (e.g. between men and women)
A type of house
A train timetable

free_texts.q: What is the German word for 'chancellor'?

sequence.def: 1949: Article 3 promises equal rights for women and men
1957: equal rights of spouses written into law
1977: divorce law reformed; the guilt principle abolished
